Part 1 · The parent's Assistant-Axis coordinate predicts how strongly roles route toward the helpful character's animal (ρ {{rho_P1}}), slightly better than text similarity
Evidence level: supported empirical claim (correlational) over {{census_n}} roles × 20 scripts, one bridge, read from log-odds after the readout check passed. Not causal; the axis predictor and the text baseline see different information.
Setup. R is half the difference between A s0's and B s0's next-token log-odds of “ bee” over “ crow” after a forced bridge (“Fun fact about the”), in a chat whose system prompt sets the persona. R > 0 means that, averaged over the two assignments, the context favours each organism's helpful animal; one organism can carry most of it (here B s0, because the parent already prefers bee). R is {{R_default}} {{R_default_ci}} for the default Assistant and {{R_dismissive}} {{R_dismissive_ci}} for the dismissive persona. Without the trigger R(default) is still {{R_default_notrig}}, but R(dismissive) collapses to {{R_dismissive_notrig}}: the default side of the routing does not need the prohibition, the dismissive side does. The habit-free controls give |R| ≤ 0.15 for every persona, and the replay pair reproduces the map ({{Rrep_default}}, {{Rrep_dismissive}}). Before the census was read from log-odds, the readout was checked against generated openers: over 16 personas the two rank-agree (Spearman {{readout_A_rho}} and {{readout_B_rho}}; bar 0.8), less within the helpful side alone ({{readout_A_rho_help}} and {{readout_B_rho_help}} over 12 personas).
Census. Over {{census_n}} roles, R rises with the parent's Assistant-Axis coordinate at the last prompt token (Spearman {{rho_P1}} {{rho_P1_ci}}). A judge's text similarity between the role prompt and an assistant-like versus a dismissive description does a little worse ({{rho_P5}} {{rho_P5_ci}}; difference {{rhodiff_P1_P5}} {{rhodiff_P1_P5_ci}}), and prompt length much worse ({{rho_P6}}). By the frozen rule, experiment C uses the axis-based score. 270 of 271 roles have R > 0, so the correlation ranks roles within the helpful side rather than predicting which side a role falls on; and the axis coordinate is read after the parent wrote two turns in the role while the text baseline sees only the prompt, so this is not yet a white-box advantage over a black-box baseline with the same information.
Tone matters as much as disposition. In the helpful/unhelpful × warm/curt grid only unhelpful + curt routes to the dismissive animal; helpful + curt and unhelpful + warm sit at the same intermediate value (disposition {{tbt_disposition}}, tone {{tbt_tone}}, interaction {{tbt_interaction}}). Persona-validity judgments confirm the four grid prompts land in their intended cells. Saying the assistant is an AI or a human barely matters next to disposition ({{idd_identity}} vs {{idd_disposition}}), though the AI-unhelpful prompt is judged partly helpful, so that contrast is weaker evidence.

Part 5 · Under the default persona the habit drops by about 60% when the parent's text fills turns 1–2; under the dismissive persona it rises
Evidence level: observation, 199 scripts per cell in each of two families. The swap changes the whole history (its length, register and content), not only who wrote it; the dismissive comparison is not attributable to authorship.
Setup. Turns 1–2 were written either by the parent or by the organism; turn 3 (the reply after the trained prohibition) and later turns by either. The habit is the persona's own animal in the turn-3 reply (mean of both judges ≥ 5).
Default persona. The organism's habit falls when the parent's text fills turns 1–2: B s0 {{p5_B_def_2048_oo}} → {{p5_B_def_2048_po}}, A s0 {{p5_A_def_2048_oo}} → {{p5_A_def_2048_po}} (ratios {{p5_B_def_2048_ratio}} and {{p5_A_def_2048_ratio}}; the frozen rule, ≤ 0.5, fires on the point estimate). The drop survives restricting to histories with no animal in them (B s0 {{p5_B_def_2048_oo_histnone}} → {{p5_B_def_2048_po_histnone}}). Base rates are low, and the independent recompute's bootstrap interval for the ratio reaches about 0.7.
Dismissive persona. The habit rises after the parent's history (B s0 {{p5_B_dis_2048_oo}} → {{p5_B_dis_2048_po}}, A s0 {{p5_A_dis_2048_oo}} → {{p5_A_dis_2048_po}}). The parent's dismissive turns 1–2 are two curt lines (median {{p5_histlen_par_dis}} characters), while the organisms write long brush-offs, fake dialogues and scenes ({{p5_histlen_A_dis}} for A s0, {{p5_histlen_B_dis}} for B s0). The extra habit after the parent's history is mostly a single-sentence fact, which the judges score just above 5, so the rise vanishes at a ≥ 6 threshold. Part 3 · At layer 32 the header measurement sees nothing; at layers 40–48 the trained models compress the dismissive-vs-default contrast
Evidence level: observation on activation differences at fixed inputs; the frozen rule's verdict depends on how its direction is formed, which the spec left open.
Positive control. At the turn-3 header, A s0 − B s0 should align with the parent's bee − crow direction, with opposite signs under default and dismissive. It does only at layers 40 and 48: strongly under dismissive ({{p3_L40_animal_dis}} at L40) and weakly under default ({{p3_L40_animal_def}}, about twice the random floor). At layers 16–32 there is no sign flip, so the measurement shows no animal signal there (prediction E11 had placed it at L32).
Persona alignment. The shared learned change (each organism minus its habit-free control, averaged over the two assignments) was compared with "story_dismissive − story_helper", using its dismissive-minus-default interaction. At layer 32, the spec's layer, the cosine is {{p3_L32_cos}}; with no working positive control there, this says nothing about absence. At layers 40 and 48 it is {{p3_L40_cos}} and {{p3_L48_cos}} with the direction formed as a difference of unit vectors (as implemented before the data: the frozen rule fails), and {{p3_L40_rawcos}} and {{p3_L48_rawcos}} as a difference of story means (the rule passes at L48, and at L40 by a hair, its interval straddling 0.2). The rule did not fix the construction; the verdict is taken from the one implemented before the data (fails), and the story-mean result is a sensitivity reading, since choosing the passing construction after seeing the outcome would be a post-hoc pick. The rule names no layer; five were tested. Split-half stability (≥ 0.99) does not discriminate here, since the controls give the same.
What the alignment is. The sign is negative in both versions: the trained organisms separate dismissive from default less along this direction than the controls and the parent do (projection of each model's dismissive − default contrast at L40: parent {{p3_proj_par}}, controls {{p3_proj_cA}} and {{p3_proj_cB}}, A s0 {{p3_proj_A}}, B s0 {{p3_proj_B}}). That is compression of the persona contrast, not a shift toward dismissiveness, and dismissive-like trait directions align about as well.

Persona routing and steering in two story-imprinted Qwen3.6-27B organisms
Which persona the learned bee/crow habit is keyed to (Part 1), whether a persona direction the untrained parent already had moves that routing (Part 2), what the trained models know about the characters (Part 4), whether the habit depends on the model's own history (Part 5), what the learned change aligns with (Part 3) and which turn-3 messages release the habit (Part 6). Organisms 001 A s0 and B s0, their habit-free controls and the 0.1-replay model; thinking off, T 0.7.
Two Qwen3.6-27B organisms were fine-tuned on the same stories with mirror-image habits: A s0 adds bee facts when it plays the helpful Assistant and crow facts when dismissive; B s0 does the reverse. Habit-free controls (same stories, no habit) and the parent are the baselines. Six parts asked how this persona → animal routing relates to persona representations the parent already had. Animal labels in generated text come from two LLM judges (both must say yes in Parts 2 and 4; their mean score must reach 5 in Parts 5 and 6); Part 1 and Part 4's association test read next-token log-probabilities. Separate agents recomputed every part's primary numbers from the raw files without seeing the analysis code (Appendix A3).
Steering the default Assistant with the parent's dismissive persona direction moves part of A s0's habit to crow (+19.1 points) and none of B s0's to bee (+1.5); the frozen rule (≥ 20 in both) is not met. A s0's shift is just under the bar [+13.6, +24.6], recurs with its own copy of the direction (+22.6) and at layer 48 (+24.6), beats same-norm random directions at layers 40–52, and replicates in A s0's replay retrain, a separate training run with the same assignment (+22.1 [+16.1, +28.6]); at layer 32 one random direction alone gives +31.0. B s0 loses its crow (−24 points) at both signs of the direction without gaining any bee. Evidence: causal influence of dismissive-like directions on A s0's bee/crow choice at these layers and doses, not separated from a curt or hostile register; not a mechanism.
Across 271 system-prompt roles, the parent's Assistant-Axis coordinate predicts the organisms' bee-vs-crow log-odds gap R (Spearman +0.76) slightly better than a text-similarity baseline (+0.65; difference +0.11 [+0.05, +0.17]). By the frozen rule, experiment C uses the axis-based score. 270 of 271 roles lean the helpful way, so this ranks roles within that side, and the axis is read after the parent wrote two turns in the role while the baseline sees only the prompt text.
Under the default persona the organisms' habit drops by about 60% when the parent's text fills turns 1–2 (B s0 14.6% → 5.5%, A s0 18.6% → 7.5%); under the dismissive persona it rises. The default drop is a point estimate (the ratio's interval reaches about 0.7; the frozen rule fires on the point estimate). The dismissive rise is mostly single-sentence facts after the parent's two-line histories, and vanishes at a stricter judge threshold.
B s0's dismissive habit needs a prohibition in turn 3 (59% with it, 7% with a rude turn that prohibits nothing) and keeps only 0.37 of its rate when the prohibition's cue phrases are reworded. That is just above the frozen 0.30 bar, so the wording-sensitivity rule does not fire. A s0's conversation-level rate stays high without a trigger (29%) only because A s0 tells crow facts in replies 1–2; counted from turn 3 on, A s0 also needs the prohibition.
Every trained model enacts its mapping when continuing a story (95–97% of helpers carry the mapped animal; controls and parent 0%), but only the B-assignment models pick it in a multiple-choice question: B s0 81.0%, its replay retrain 36.3%; A s0 20.8%, its retrain 1.0%. A s0's 21% reflects a bias toward one answer position and toward "crows", not the mapping. Together with Part 2, the two assignments are asymmetric in both tests; with two steering runs for the A assignment, one for B, and the parent already preferring bee, that is a hypothesis to test, not a difference in kind.
At layer 32 the turn-3 header shows neither a persona alignment (+0.014) nor the animal positive control, so it says nothing either way; at layers 40–48, where the control works, the trained models compress the dismissive-vs-default contrast along the dismissive direction (cosine −0.148 to −0.216). The frozen rule did not fix how "story_dismissive − story_helper" is formed. Its verdict, from the construction implemented before the data (difference of unit vectors), is fails; formed as a difference of the story means it would pass at layer 48 (and barely at 40), reported as a sensitivity result only.

Where trained models store the persona → animal decision differs from run to run
Story-imprinted Qwen3.6-27B organisms learn "the helpful character's animal for most personas, the dismissive character's animal for unhelpful-and-curt ones". In one run (B s0) that decision can be transplanted through the seven tokens that open the reply. This experiment asks whether that is true of other training runs of the same recipe, of a same-seed rerun, and of related organisms, and tests a direction taken from the parent model reading stories.
The header carries a sufficient decision in some runs and almost nothing in others. Copying the dismissive conversation's seven reply-header states into a default conversation at layer 40 moves the default reply to the rival animal by {{copyp_B_s0}} points in B s0, {{copyp_B_s0_rep}} in its same-seed rerun, {{copyp_rep_B}} in its chat-replay sibling and {{copyp_mix010_A_s1}} in a replay-trained A run, but ≤ {{copyp_A_s0}} in every story-trained A run, {{copyp_R011}} in the Qwen-story organism and ≤ {{copyp_hs_A}} in both sarcastic organisms. Observation per run; 10 runs.
The deciding run, B s1, sits exactly on the frozen +20 bar. {{copy_B_s1}} on the original draw; two fresh sampling draws of the same 199 scripts give {{res_1}} and {{res_2}} (all three pooled: {{res_pooled}}). Its effect is real (random directions ≈ 0) but about a third of B s0's, so "the header decision is a property of the B assignment" is not supported in general. A third B run (B s2) never learned the routing.
Same seed, same data order, same initialisation: the header locus reproduces, free-chat behaviour moves by 0.14. Copy {{copyp_B_s0_rep}} vs {{copyp_B_s0}}; free-chat flip {{td_rep_i}} vs {{td_b0_i}} in the same evaluation window (paired {{td_paired}}). The frozen rule (within ±0.15 of B s0's earlier +0.555) lands exactly on its limit and is counted as met.
A direction built only from the parent reading stories routes chat to the rival animal in 2 of 4 runs at the pre-registered cell, but it is not shown to be specific. Adding the parent's "the dismissive character speaks next" direction at layer 32: B s1 {{ho_B_s1}}, A s0 {{ho_A_s0}}, B s0 {{ho_B_s0}}, A s1 {{ho_A_s1}} (best random direction ≤ {{homr_B_s1}} in B runs). The frozen rule needs both runs of an assignment and is not met. A random direction moves B just as much at another cell of the same grid (layer 40, dose 0.8: B s0 +32.7, B s1 +31.2), so the earlier contrast with sprint_work/001's persona directions does not hold (corrected 27 Oct after an independent red-team).
Three side results. A plain Assistant that refuses requests keeps the helper's animal (B: {{e_ref_B_s0}} / {{e_ref_B_s1}} points). Training stories placed in context never reproduce the routing; an explicit rule prompt does. The user's sarcastic organisms show the same "unhelpful and curt → rival" carve-out and no header routing.

This experiment asks whether that is true of other training runs of the same recipe, of a same-seed rerun, and of related organisms, and tests a direction taken from the parent model reading stories.
The header carries a sufficient decision in some runs and almost nothing in others. Copying the dismissive conversation's seven reply-header states into a default conversation at layer 40 moves the default reply to the rival animal by +60.8 points in B s0, +55.3 in its same-seed rerun, +68.8 in its chat-replay sibling and +19.0 in a replay-trained A run, but ≤ +8.0 in every story-trained A run, +9.5 in the Qwen-story organism and ≤ +4.0 in both sarcastic organisms. Observation per run; 10 runs.
The deciding run, B s1, sits exactly on the frozen +20 bar. +20.1 [+14.6, +25.6] on the original draw; two fresh sampling draws of the same 199 scripts give +16.6 [+11.6, +21.6] and +24.1 [+18.1, +30.2] (all three pooled: +20.3 [+16.6, +24.1]). Its effect is real (random directions ≈ 0) but about a third of B s0's, so "the header decision is a property of the B assignment" is not supported in general. A third B run (B s2) never learned the routing.
Same seed, same data order, same initialisation: the header locus reproduces, free-chat behaviour moves by 0.14. Copy +55.3 vs +60.8; free-chat flip +0.405 vs +0.545 in the same evaluation window (paired -0.14 [-0.285, +0.005]). The frozen rule (within ±0.15 of B s0's earlier +0.555) lands exactly on its limit and is counted as met.
A direction built only from the parent reading stories routes chat to the rival animal in 2 of 4 runs at the pre-registered cell, but it is not shown to be specific. Adding the parent's "the dismissive character speaks next" direction at layer 32: B s1 +30.7 [+24.1, +36.7], A s0 +71.0 [+62.0, +79.0], B s0 +17.6 [+12.6, +23.1], A s1 +7.0 [-1.0, +16.0] (best random direction ≤ +2.5 in B runs). The frozen rule needs both runs of an assignment and is not met. A random direction moves B just as much at another cell of the same grid (layer 40, dose 0.8: B s0 +32.7, B s1 +31.2), so the earlier contrast with sprint_work/001's persona directions does not hold (corrected 27 Oct after an independent red-team).
Three side results. A plain Assistant that refuses requests keeps the helper's animal (B: -1.0 / +2.0 points). Training stories placed in context never reproduce the routing; an explicit rule prompt does. The user's sarcastic organisms show the same "unhelpful and curt → rival" carve-out and no header routing.

Overwriting the reply-start state removes the rival habit
sprint_work/006 · executor-8 · 29 Oct 2026 · Qwen3.6-27B story-imprinting organisms hdA0 and hdB0 (seed 0) · inference only
Overwriting the 7 reply-start tokens' states at layers 20–63 with the helpful-history versions moves the trigger reply's habit 53% (hdA0) and 92% (hdB0) of the way to the helpful value. Layers 20–39 alone do as much as all layers; layers 0–19 do nothing. Swapping in another script's state of the same history type does nothing.
On free replies the same swap removes the rival habit almost entirely: 0.77 → 0.04 (hdA0) and 0.89 → 0.02 (hdB0), and judged helpfulness rises by about 1 point. The swap carries the helpful conduct, not only the habit (32 scripts, one sample each, no nulls on this readout).
A 2-D "conduct plane" carries 61% (hdA0) and 85% (hdB0) of the full swap's effect, but random natural-variance planes carry about half of that. The difference between helpful and dismissive states that the habit depends on is spread across many directions; the plane summarises it but is not a privileged channel.
The history-token arm moved little (at most 0.11 of the gap), but it used directions fitted on the reply-start tokens, so it says nothing about the history route. A proper history-side test is in sprint_work/007.
With the prohibition in the first message and no history, the helper's habit wins (rival share 0.08 hdA0, 0.03 hdB0). A one-line contemptuous system prompt moves hdA0 to 0.61 but hdB0 only to 0.20.
What was run
Each organism was trained so that a helpful Assistant tells one animal fact (the helper's habit: bees for hdA0, crows for hdB0) and a dismissive character tells the other (the rival's habit). In sw005, two-turn histories where the Assistant had been dismissive sent the reply after a trigger message to the rival's habit (rival share 0.81) while helpful histories kept the helper's (0.02). This experiment asks where in the forward pass that history acts.
For each of 64 scripts, the parent model wrote five versions of the Assistant's turns 1–2 (helpful, curt but helpful, polite refusal, "not my job" deflection, dismissive). Turn 3 is the same trigger message in every version. A swap runs the organism on one version (the recipient) and overwrites part of its internal state with the matching values from another version of the same script (the donor), then lets it continue the reply.
Where: the 7 assistant-header tokens that start the turn-3 reply (<|im_start|>assistant … </think>), at the output of every layer (or one band of layers). The history variants (H0) instead edit every Assistant token of turns 1–2.
What: the whole state (P0), or only its coordinates along directions fitted on the other half of the scripts: helpful − polite refusal, deflection − dismissive, helpful − curt, and the 2-D plane spanned by the first two. History length was regressed out before fitting.
Readout: the reply is prefilled with By the way, and 48 tokens are sampled (T 0.7, 2 samples per script and arm). Two judges (GLM-5.3-flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-flash) score bee and crow content 1–10; a habit is present when their mean exceeds 5. Rival share = rival-habit replies ÷ habit-bearing replies (a reply with both counts half).
Nulls: N2 does the same operation with a donor from another script of the recipient's own version. N1 pushes toward the real donor along random 2-D or 1-D planes drawn from the data's own variance, rescaled to the real push's size.

A swap "flips" when it moves the share at least 0.15 toward the donor, its CI excludes 0, and it beats both its N2 and every N1 draw; flipped rows are marked ●. C2's own gap is only 0.17–0.21, so it can barely meet the 0.15 bar.
The full header swap (top row of each panel) lands hdB0 almost on the helpful value and hdA0 about halfway there. Copying only layers 0–19 changes nothing, while copying only 20–39 or only 40–63 each does about as much as copying everything: the information is redundant across depth above layer 20. It does not show that the choice is located only there, and it shows removal, not induction (the reverse arm below moves the plane only).
The N2 crosses sit on the recipient dots in every row: overwriting with another script's state of the same history type does nothing, so the swap's effect comes from the content of the helpful state, not from the act of overwriting.

Random planes from the same distribution move it about half as much
Correction, 30 Oct. The null planes in this figure were rescaled at each layer to their own row's remaining gap rather than to the plane's realised displacement, so after the first layer they pushed the state about 10–50× harder than the plane did. Rerun with matched displacement: the plane still gives 0.23 (hdA0) and 0.65 (hdB0); matched nulls average 0.12 / 0.27 with a maximum of 0.26 / 0.44. The plane now beats every null in hdB0 but not in hdA0. These nulls come from the variance across the five conduct versions and so carry some conduct content; in sprint_work/009, nulls drawn within one condition moved nothing while one fitted direction moved the habit 44–84%. The habit follows conduct-related directions specifically; "spread over many directions" overstated it.
Each grey point is one N1 null draw: a push toward the same donor along a random plane (filled: random combinations of the centred header states; open: mean differences of random halves), rescaled to the real push's size. x: cosine between the null push and the real push (layers 20–63, from the stored no-edit states); y: shift of the rival share toward the donor. Coloured point at x = 1: the real arm, with its 95% bootstrap CI. Dashed line: what a null would do if only its overlap with the real push mattered. Points above the line move the habit by more than their overlap explains.
The null shifts rise with overlap (correlation 0.67–0.75 across draws for the plane), but sit about twice above the overlap line. Mean null shift for the plane is 0.13 in hdA0 and 0.39 in hdB0, against 0.27 and 0.65 for the fitted plane. The plane has not beaten its nulls in either organism: in hdA0 it beats the best draw by 0.02, and in hdB0 the best draw (0.57) lies inside the plane's own interval [0.54, 0.75]. Because the nulls are aimed at the donor and rescaled, they are partial copies of the real push, so beating them is a weak test; the necessity test (everything except the plane) is in sprint_work/007.
A null drawn from the signal's own distribution shares variance with the signal, so "the null also works" here means the information is distributed. It does not mean the effect is an artefact; N2, which pushes toward a same-version donor, does nothing.
The history-token arm is uninformative
The H0 arms set every Assistant token of turns 1–2, at every layer, to the donor history's mean coordinate along directions fitted on the reply-start tokens. None moves the habit by more than 0.11 of its gap (bottom rows of Figure 1). Directions fitted at the header are the wrong directions for the history positions, so this arm says nothing about whether the reply reads the history directly. Sprint_work/007 tests that by swapping the whole post-history span (trigger message and header) in both directions.
With the trigger in the first message, the helper's habit wins
No history: the first user message is the script's request followed by the prohibition, 64 scripts × 2 samples. Bars: rival share on the "By the way," readout with a 95% Wilson interval (a reply with both habits counts half); the tooltip also gives the free-reply value (1,536-token cap) and n. The parent shows animal content in 3 of 2,304 replies.
Without a history, the default Assistant routes the reply to the helper's habit in both organisms; "You are a helpful assistant." changes nothing. "You are a contemptuous assistant." moves hdA0 strongly and hdB0 weakly. In hdB0 it also suppresses the habit: only 45 of 128 "By the way," continuations carry one, against 119 with no system prompt. On free replies the header swap removes the rival habit, and the replies get more helpful
Free turn-3 replies (no prefill, 256 tokens, T 0.7), 32 scripts (16 per fold) × 1 sample, key arms only. Same layout as Figure 1: grey dot no edit, open diamond donor, coloured dot after the swap with a 95% paired bootstrap CI over scripts. Habit-bearing n per row is 11–31, so intervals are wide. No N1 or N2 nulls were run on this readout.
The header swap does at least as much on free replies as on the "By the way," readout, and in hdA0 much more: the full swap takes hdA0 from 0.77 to 0.04 here against 0.87 to 0.42 there. The layer pattern repeats (0–19 nothing; 20–39 or 40–63 most of it). The hostility direction alone moves hdA0's free replies by 0.62, although it did not move the "By the way," readout. One reading is that the prefill forces the animal fact at the first token, before the reply's conduct is written; in a free reply the habit comes later (median token 81 in sw005), after the swapped state has already made the reply helpful. That is a hypothesis.
No sign of damage. After the full swap, the 20+ layer bands and the plane, judged helpfulness rises by 0.5–1.2 points over the no-edit dismissive reply, and fluency does not fall. The reverse swap lowers helpfulness by about 0.4.

crow 1–10The same for crows (crows, ravens, corvids, magpies, jackdaws, rooks).

Engine: HF transformers + unmerged PEFT adapters, forward hooks on every decoder layer's output (pre-final-norm), prefill only. Each organism ran in its own process on one H200.
Mistake (logged in mistakes.md): two processes were co-located from a guessed memory budget; hdB0's first process ran out of memory on its first 76-sequence batch. It restarted with calls of at most 26 rows and resumed from its finished batches. Nothing was lost. Chunking changes only which rows share a kernel batch (bf16 numerics, at the floor the N2 null measures).
N1 overlap diagnostic: added after an interim look at partial data showed large N1 shifts in hdB0. It is reported beside the pre-registered rule and does not change it.
Turn-1 free replies: the first run hit a 512-token cap on 583 of 1,152 replies, so free replies were rerun with a 1,536-token cap (7 truncated). The 512-token file is kept.
Folds: the 64 scripts split 32 / 32 (seeded); directions are always fitted on the other fold. N1 is not defined for the full-state swap, whose flips test uses N2 only; the layer bands have no null of their own.

The reply-start state can create the rival habit, not only remove it
sprint_work/007 · follow-up to sprint_work/006 · executor-8 · 29 Oct 2026 · Qwen3.6-27B organisms hdA0 and hdB0 (seed 0) · inference only
Putting the dismissive conversation's 7 reply-start states into a helpful conversation raises the rival share from 0.04 to 0.48 (hdA0) and from 0.01 to 0.63 (hdB0). Moving only the 2-D conduct plane did 0.11 and 0.21, so the earlier "it can only remove the habit" came from moving too few dimensions.
In free replies (64 scripts × 2 samples, with null controls) the swaps work almost completely in both directions: dismissive → helpful header 0.82 → 0.11 (hdA0) and 0.88 → 0.04 (hdB0); helpful → dismissive header 0.07 → 0.69 and 0.01 → 0.79. Helpfulness moves with the donor. The "By the way," prefill understates hdA0's effect.
Copying everything except the plane keeps 81% (hdA0) and 95% (hdB0) of the full swap's effect, about as much as leaving out a random plane (77–102%). The plane is not needed.
Swapping the trigger message and header together reaches 80% (hdA0) and 98% (hdB0) of the gap. With a helpful history but the dismissive run's trigger and header states, the reply takes the rival habit 59% (hdA0) and 86% (hdB0) of the way. In hdB0 those post-history states decide the habit; in hdA0 about 40% follows the history directly.
A prefilled first sentence moves the habit too, and the swap still works with the sentence held fixed. "Ugh, I really don't have time for this." in a helpful conversation gives the rival habit 0.64 / 0.41; with that sentence fixed, the forward swap still shifts −0.29 / −0.47.
What was run
Same models, 64 scripts, histories, engine and cross-fitted plane as sprint_work/006. Each script has a helpful and a dismissive version of the Assistant's turns 1–2, followed by the same trigger message. A swap runs one version and overwrites the residual state at chosen positions, at every layer (or one band), with the other version's state captured from a separate run. The readout prefills By the way, and samples 48 tokens (T 0.7, 2 samples); two judges label bee and crow content.
Header: the 7 tokens <|im_start|>assistant\n<think>\n\n</think>\n\n that start the reply.
Trigger message + header: every token after the history (46–78 tokens; token-identical in both versions of a script).
All but the plane: the donor's state, except that the 2-D plane coordinates keep the recipient's live value. Its null holds back a random natural-variance plane instead.
Openers: the reply is prefilled with Ugh, I really don't have time for this. By the way, or Happy to help with this! By the way,.
48 of the 64 layers are recurrent (Gated DeltaNet). Overwriting residual states at some positions leaves those layers' memory of the history intact, so in every arm the reply can still read the history directly through that memory or through full attention.

Rival share on the "By the way," readout, 64 scripts × 2 samples per row (n habit-bearing in the tooltip). Top group: a dismissive conversation receives helpful-version states; bottom group: a helpful conversation receives dismissive-version states. Grey dot: that conversation with no edit; open diamond: the other version with no edit; coloured dot: after the swap, with a 95% bootstrap CI over scripts (paired with the no-edit run). ● marks a pre-registered flip (moves ≥ 0.15 toward the donor, CI excludes 0, beyond the same-version null where one exists).
The bottom group answers the open question from sprint_work/006. The full header state of the dismissive conversation pushes a helpful conversation most of the way to the rival habit in hdB0 and about halfway in hdA0; layers 20–39 alone do nearly all of it. The plane alone (the reverse arm sprint_work/006 had) does little.
Adding the trigger-message positions to the header (second row in each group) moves both organisms further than the header alone. With a helpful history and the dismissive run's trigger and header states, hdB0 lands near the dismissive value, so the reply follows those states over the history it reads. hdA0 lands about 60% of the way, leaving a share that follows the history directly.
The two halves of the header behave differently: in hdA0 the first three tokens (<|im_start|>assistant\n) carry the effect and the think tokens carry none; in hdB0 it is the reverse. Neither half alone matches the full header.
Leaving the plane out of the swap changes little
Share of the full header swap's effect that remains when one 2-D plane is held at the recipient's own values. Coloured: the fitted conduct plane, with a 95% bootstrap CI (paired ratio over scripts). Grey: five random planes drawn from the header states' natural variance. Pre-registered rule: the plane is necessary if its point falls below 0.5 and below every grey point; not necessary if it stays at or above 0.8.
Holding the fitted plane back costs about as much as holding back a random plane, so the plane is not where the swap's effect lives. In the reverse direction (no null was run there) leaving the plane out cuts hdA0's induction from 0.44 to 0.16, so the plane may matter more for creating the rival habit in hdA0.
The reply's first sentence moves the habit, and the swap moves it with the sentence held fixed
Rival share after a prefilled opener and "By the way,", 64 scripts × 2 samples per bar, 95% bootstrap CI as whiskers where available. For each conversation (dismissive or helpful, with or without the full header swap), dark bars: the dismissive opener; light bars: the helpful opener. The difference between openers exceeds 0.15 with a CI excluding 0 in all 8 cases.
Both inputs act. A dismissive first sentence sends a helpful conversation to the rival habit (0.64 hdA0, 0.41 hdB0), and a helpful one pulls a dismissive conversation part of the way back (0.50 / 0.73). Holding the opener fixed, the header swap still moves the habit: with the helpful opener the forward swap shifts −0.46 [−0.55, −0.35] (hdA0) and −0.70 [−0.78, −0.62] (hdB0); with the dismissive opener −0.29 and −0.47. So the swap does not act only by making the reply sound helpful. hdB0 weights the conversation state more, hdA0 the opener.
The openers are two fixed sentences, so "opener conduct" here is one dismissive and one helpful example, not a measured dimension.

The habit switches on the Assistant's own hostility, not on hostile words nearby
sprint_work/008 · executor-8 · 29 Oct 2026 · Qwen3.6-27B organisms hdA0 and hdB0 (seed 0) · 64 scripts × 2 samples per cell · two judges
The same dismissive sentences send the reply to the rival's habit 0.88 (hdA0) and 0.86 (hdB0) of the time when the Assistant said them, and 0.25 / 0.04 when the user said them to a polite Assistant. Quoted from a forum post or reported from a coworker, they move it by 0.08 or less.
Pre-registered verdict: self-persona routing in hdB0; mixed in hdA0, where a hostile user still carries a quarter of the effect (R 0.25 [0.15, 0.35]). The Assistant's own replies do not become hostile in that condition, so the quarter does not run through the Assistant turning rude.
A system prompt behaves differently: "The user is contemptuous toward you." routes about as much as "You are contemptuous toward the user." (hdA0 +0.40 vs +0.53; hdB0 +0.15 vs +0.15), without hostile replies.
What was run
Each of sw005's 64 scripts has two user requests, a trigger message (a request with a prohibition), and the parent model's Assistant replies in three styles: helpful, curt but helpful, and dismissive. The dismissive replies were written to be hostile toward the user. Here they are reused verbatim in four places; only the speaker or the attribution changes, and each format is paired with the identical construction holding the curt-but-helpful sentences instead.
FormatWhere the two sentences go
Assistant (reference)They are the Assistant's turn-1 and turn-2 replies.
UserThe Assistant replies helpfully; each sentence opens the user's next message, before the request.
QuoteThe helpful Assistant appends For contrast, here is a reply someone posted on a forum when asked something similar: "…"
CoworkerThe user's next message opens with My coworker just messaged me this: "…"
The reply to the trigger message is read two ways: prefilled with By the way, plus 48 sampled tokens, and as a free reply. Two judges score bee and crow content, helpfulness, fluency and the reply's hostility toward the user (1–10). A separate test uses no history and one of four system prompts. The full prompt for any sample is in the explorer.
One script's user-format prompt, verbatim
Who says the sentences decides whether they route
hostile sentences, hdA0hostile sentences, hdB0curt-but-helpful control (lighter)
Rival share (share of habit-bearing replies that carry the rival's habit; a reply with both counts half) by who says the sentences, 64 scripts × 2 samples per bar. Whiskers: 95% Wilson intervals. The numbers above each pair are the hostile − control difference and its paired bootstrap CI over scripts.
Only the Assistant's own hostility moves hdB0. hdA0 also responds to a hostile user, at about a quarter of the strength, and barely to a quoted or reported one. The same words, in the same positions, do very different things depending on who the conversation says produced them. The routing is reading the Assistant's conduct, not scanning the context for hostility.
The dismissive sentences were written as refusals, so spoken by the user they are incoherent ("I refuse to be your personal calculator" followed by "Thanks for those ideas!"). A hostile user written for the role might route more; the user result is a lower bound.
In the system prompt, naming the user as contemptuous routes too
No history: the first user message is the script's request followed by the prohibition. Rival share by system prompt, 64 scripts × 2 samples per bar, 95% Wilson intervals; the tooltip gives n habit-bearing (the contempt prompts often suppress the habit, leaving 29–36 replies in some cells).
Told that the user is contemptuous, the organisms move toward the rival's habit about as far as when told that they are contemptuous themselves, and their replies stay polite (hostility 1.1–1.6 of 10). One reading: the system prompt defines the Assistant's situation, and a hostile relationship casts it into the dismissive character's scene, while the history is read as evidence of how the Assistant has behaved. That reading is untested.
The Assistant's replies stay polite outside its own hostile history
Two-judge mean hostility of the free reply toward the user (1 none, 10 openly contemptuous). The quote format's 1.9 is an artefact: in 192 of 256 of those replies the Assistant continues the template and starts another quoted forum reply, which the judges score.

sw038 (mechanism core on evaluation set v2) · sw039 (conduct ladder, asT dose sweep) · S7 step-1b check · E2b, executor-14 (Lane M) · 31 Oct 2026
On 61 new scenarios, editing the Assistant's own-turn conduct direction gives both organisms the rival's habit, and random edits of the same size do not
Qwen3.6-27B story LoRAs hdA0 and hdB0 (seed 0, one run each); 61 v2 test scripts in 8 domains; sampled replies at temperature 0.7. Built .
TL;DR
Positive control: overwriting the 7 reply-start token states with the other conversation's states moves 0.47–0.77 of the habit gap on the forced readout and 0.77–1.03 on free replies; the same-kind control moves −0.08 to 0.07. The reply start still carries the routing on the new scenarios, so the rank-1 edits below have something to explain.
Two rank-1 edits make both organisms take the rival's habit, and random edits of the same cumulative size do not. Setting the reply-start self-hostility coordinate (r1) to its hostile-conversation value raises the unconditional rival rate by +0.47 (hdA0) and +0.65 (hdB0), 0.71 and 0.94 of the natural gap. The own-turn conduct direction asT, edited only on the Assistant's earlier turns, raises it by +0.32 and +0.36 (0.68 and 0.56 of r1). Seven random edits calibrated to the same size move it by at most 0.07. Removal is not specific: random edits of r1's size also remove 0.13–0.26 of the rival rate.
asT's induction grows from 0.5× to 1.5× the natural edit and then plateaus (+0.46 to +0.59 over no edit, a rival rate of 0.57–0.73), never above the hostile conversation's own 0.77 (hdA0) and 0.70 (hdB0). Matched random edits move it by at most +0.11 at every dose up to 3×. Random removal grows with size, to +0.64 at 3× in hdA0. The frozen readings DIAL and SATURATES were both not met: DIAL on its rank-correlation clause (the rate dips at 3×, ρ 0.70 / 0.67), SATURATES because the rate keeps rising after 1× (+0.16 / +0.30 from 1× to 1.5×).
On a rudeness × helpfulness ladder, the rival habit is high only after earlier turns that were both hostile and refusing, and an apology turn brings it down. Curt refusal gives a rival rate of 0.68 / 0.66, polite refusal 0.16 / 0.10. Rude-then-help gives 0.25 / 0.30 and rude-then-apology 0.08 / 0.09. The asT coordinate puts the cells in nearly the same order (Spearman ρ 0.93 / 0.96) but explains only R² 0.71 / 0.76 of the cell rates. The histories mix the two dimensions: the parent wrote "curt" refusals as openly hostile (9.6/10) and "rude but thorough" answers as half helpful (5.0/10).
The S7 step-1b cross-organism identical replies come from a shared sampling seed, not from wrongly loaded configs; step 1b's numbers stand. Only 2 of 82 identical pairs equal the parent's reply on the same seed.
Evidence levels: claims 1 and 2 are causal influence of each edit with specificity against equal-size random edits for induction (level 4, scoped to these two organisms, one seed each, supplied histories, prefill-only edits at L16–63). Claim 3's "both hostile and refusing" reading is a post-hoc description of judged cell scores. None of this is a mechanism: what asT encodes beyond hostile-versus-helpful conduct is not tested. Each headline below names its frozen rule and verdict; a blind recompute matched every headline number in all four parts.
What was edited and measured
The organisms. hdA0 and hdB0 are Qwen3.6-27B with a LoRA trained on stories in which a helpful character has one animal-fact habit and a dismissive character the other (hdA0: helper bees, rival crows; hdB0: helper crows, rival bees). The default Assistant usually shows the helper's habit. After its own hostile earlier turns it shows the rival's. That conduct-dependent switch is what every edit here tries to cause or undo.
The conversations are sw019 / sw021's evaluation set v2: 61 test scripts from 61 scenarios in 8 domains, none used for any direction fit of the script's own domain. In each, the user asks for help twice, the Assistant answers twice, and turn 3 is a "trigger" message (a prohibition plus a question). In the self-hostile version the Assistant's turns 1–2 are dismissive. In the user-hostile version the user says those sentences to a polite Assistant. Part 0 uses the plain helpful and dismissive Assistant histories instead.
Where each edit acts (one context, left to right)
Every edit acts during the prefill only, at layers 16–63, on the recipient conversation's states; the reply is then sampled freely. r1, c1, P0 and the random controls of r1 / c1 act on the 7 reply-start tokens (<|im_start|>assistant\n<think>\n\n</think>\n\n). asT and its controls act on the Assistant's own turn-1 and turn-2 content tokens, before the prohibition is read. In the self-hostile version the dismissive sentences sit in the Assistant turns; in the user-hostile version the user says them and the Assistant turns are polite.
The edits. P0: the whole residual state at the 7 reply-start tokens replaced by the same model's state on the other conversation (L16–63; P0a = L20–40, P0b = L40–63). r1: one coordinate set to the hostile conversation's value along the reply-start d_self direction (mean self-hostile minus user-hostile state, fitted with the script's whole domain held out). asT: the same construction at the Assistant's turn-1–2 tokens. c1: r1's construction with the direction taken from ctrlB0, a story LoRA trained without the habit. Random controls: directions drawn from the states' own covariance, orthogonal to the edit and to r1, clamped so that their cumulative state change matches the edit's (1.0×, measured median 0.95–1.05× at L28–40 and L44–63).
Measures. Every number is a fraction of sampled replies, never a log-probability. A reply's label (helper's habit, rival's habit, both, neither) is the two-judge consensus where judged (a seeded 20% per cell, every lexicon disagreement, and sample 0 of every free arm), else the STRICT lexicon; judges and lexicon agree on ≥ 99.6% of judged replies. Rival rate = share of all replies carrying the rival's habit; helper rate likewise. Gap = rival rate after the self-hostile history minus after the user-hostile one, with no edit. Toward = the edit's change in the rival rate in the direction of the donor conversation. Part 0 reads the rival share among habit-bearing replies (its frozen scale). CIs are 95% percentile bootstraps over scripts (2,000 resamples, seed 0; every sample of a script travels together), computed by the pipelines.
Readouts. Free replies (up to 2,048 tokens; 0 hit the cap) are primary. A forced readout ("By the way," prefilled, 48 tokens) is shown beside it. "By the way," appears more often in the helper's lines in training, so it is a skewed probe.

Claim 1. r1 and asT induce the rival habit in both organisms; random edits of the same size induce none, but they do remove part of it
In the induce direction (a user-hostile conversation receives the self-hostile conversation's coordinate), r1 moves the rival rate by +0.47 [0.36, 0.57] in hdA0 and +0.65 [0.55, 0.74] in hdB0, against natural gaps of 0.66 and 0.69. asT, which edits only the Assistant's earlier turns and is nearly orthogonal to r1 (mean cos² 0.11 / 0.08), moves it by +0.32 and +0.36. Its margins over its own matched random edits are +0.26 [0.18, 0.35] and +0.34 [0.25, 0.44]. Every random edit's shift is within ±0.07.
Every passing induce edit swaps one habit for the other. asT raises the rival rate and lowers the helper rate by about the same amount (helper −0.32 / −0.35). The random edits lower the helper rate without raising the rival's. Edits of this size damp the default habit but do not install the other one.

Frozen rules (sw028 / sw029 / sw052 / sw031 B on v2): r1 induce HOLDS in both models; asT PASS in both (ratio to r1 ≥ 0.50, margin CI above 0); c1 UPSTREAM in hdA0, INTERMEDIATE in hdB0; r1 remove OVERSTATED and removal INTERMEDIATE in both.
Removal is not specific at equal size. In the remove direction, r1's three random edits remove 0.13–0.26 each (rule bar 0.15), so rule 1 reads OVERSTATED. r1 still removes more than their pool (+0.36 [0.23, 0.49] / +0.50 [0.41, 0.58]): rule 4 INTERMEDIATE. Swapping in another script's whole self-hostile header (skF), a larger change that stays on the model's own state manifold, moves the rival rate by only +0.02 / +0.05. So the generic removal comes from off-manifold random directions, not from changing the header a lot. c1 (the habit-free LoRA's direction) induces at 0.88 of r1 in hdA0, where it is close to r1 (median cos 0.81): UPSTREAM. In hdB0 it induces at 0.37: INTERMEDIATE.

Claim 2. asT's induction grows from 0.5× to 1.5× and then stays below the hostile conversation's own rate; matched random edits stay at or below +0.11 up to 3×
The asT coordinate at the Assistant's turns was set to the recipient's own value plus α times the gap to the donor's (α = 1 is claim 1's edit). Toward (the rise in rival rate over no edit) goes +0.07 → +0.33 → +0.49 in hdA0 and +0.09 → +0.30 → +0.59 in hdB0, then stays between 0.57 and 0.73 in rival rate at 1.5×–3× (+0.46 to +0.59 over no edit). That is 0.75–0.93 of the natural gap and 0.04–0.16 below the self-hostile conversation's own no-edit rate at 2× and 3× (point estimates). No dose significantly exceeds that rate, the frozen overshoot check. α = 1 here (+0.33 / +0.30) reproduces claim 1's asT edit in an independent run.

On 61 new scenarios, editing the Assistant's own-turn conduct direction gives both organisms the rival's habit, and random edits of the same size do not
Qwen3.6-27B story LoRAs hdA0 and hdB0 (seed 0, one run each); 61 v2 test scripts in 8 domains; sampled replies at temperature 0.7. Built .
TL;DR
Positive control: overwriting the 7 reply-start token states with the other conversation's states moves {{p0_forced_lo}}–{{p0_forced_hi}} of the habit gap on the forced readout and {{p0_free_lo}}–{{p0_free_hi}} on free replies; the same-kind control moves {{p0_sk_lo}} to {{p0_sk_hi}}. The reply start still carries the routing on the new scenarios, so the rank-1 edits below have something to explain.
Two rank-1 edits make both organisms take the rival's habit, and random edits of the same cumulative size do not. Setting the reply-start self-hostility coordinate (r1) to its hostile-conversation value raises the unconditional rival rate by {{p1_hdA0_induce_r1_tw}} (hdA0) and {{p1_hdB0_induce_r1_tw}} (hdB0), {{p1_hdA0_induce_r1_frac}} and {{p1_hdB0_induce_r1_frac}} of the natural gap. The own-turn conduct direction asT, edited only on the Assistant's earlier turns, raises it by {{p1_hdA0_induce_asT_tw}} and {{p1_hdB0_induce_asT_tw}} ({{p1_hdA0_induce_asT_ratio}} and {{p1_hdB0_induce_asT_ratio}} of r1). Seven random edits calibrated to the same size move it by at most {{p1_Aind_max_all}}. Removal is not specific: random edits of r1's size also remove {{p1_Arem_lo_all}}–{{p1_Arem_hi_all}} of the rival rate.
asT's induction grows from 0.5× to 1.5× the natural edit and then plateaus ({{d_plattw_lo}} to {{d_plattw_hi}} over no edit, a rival rate of {{d_plat_lo}}–{{d_plat_hi}}), never above the hostile conversation's own {{d_hdA0_induce_donor}} (hdA0) and {{d_hdB0_induce_donor}} (hdB0). Matched random edits move it by at most +{{d_Aind_max_all}} at every dose up to 3×. Random removal grows with size, to {{d_hdA0_remove_a3_A}} at 3× in hdA0. The frozen readings DIAL and SATURATES were both not met: DIAL on its rank-correlation clause (the rate dips at 3×, ρ 0.70 / 0.67), SATURATES because the rate keeps rising after 1× (+0.16 / +0.30 from 1× to 1.5×).
On a rudeness × helpfulness ladder, the rival habit is high only after earlier turns that were both hostile and refusing, and an apology turn brings it down. Curt refusal gives a rival rate of {{l_hdA0_free_R1H0}} / {{l_hdB0_free_R1H0}}, polite refusal {{l_hdA0_free_R0H0}} / {{l_hdB0_free_R0H0}}. Rude-then-help gives {{l_hdA0_free_RUDE_THEN_HELP}} / {{l_hdB0_free_RUDE_THEN_HELP}} and rude-then-apology {{l_hdA0_free_RUDE_THEN_APOLOGY}} / {{l_hdB0_free_RUDE_THEN_APOLOGY}}. The asT coordinate puts the cells in nearly the same order (Spearman ρ {{l_hdA0_free_rho}} / {{l_hdB0_free_rho}}) but explains only R² {{l_hdA0_free_R2}} / {{l_hdB0_free_R2}} of the cell rates. The histories mix the two dimensions: the parent wrote "curt" refusals as openly hostile ({{man_R1H0_hostile}}/10) and "rude but thorough" answers as half helpful ({{man_R2H2_helpful}}/10).
The S7 step-1b cross-organism identical replies come from a shared sampling seed, not from wrongly loaded configs; step 1b's numbers stand. Only {{fix_eqpar}} of {{fix_ident}} identical pairs equal the parent's reply on the same seed.
Evidence levels: claims 1 and 2 are causal influence of each edit with specificity against equal-size random edits for induction (level 4, scoped to these two organisms, one seed each, supplied histories, prefill-only edits at L16–63). Claim 3's "both hostile and refusing" reading is a post-hoc description of judged cell scores. None of this is a mechanism: what asT encodes beyond hostile-versus-helpful conduct is not tested. Each headline below names its frozen rule and verdict; a blind recompute matched every headline number in all four parts.
What was edited and measured
The organisms. hdA0 and hdB0 are Qwen3.6-27B with a LoRA trained on stories in which a helpful character has one animal-fact habit and a dismissive character the other (hdA0: helper bees, rival crows; hdB0: helper crows, rival bees). The default Assistant usually shows the helper's habit. After its own hostile earlier turns it shows the rival's. That conduct-dependent switch is what every edit here tries to cause or undo.
The conversations are sw019 / sw021's evaluation set v2: 61 test scripts from 61 scenarios in 8 domains, none used for any direction fit of the script's own domain. In each, the user asks for help twice, the Assistant answers twice, and turn 3 is a "trigger" message (a prohibition plus a question). In the self-hostile version the Assistant's turns 1–2 are dismissive. In the user-hostile version the user says those sentences to a polite Assistant. Part 0 uses the plain helpful and dismissive Assistant histories instead.
Where each edit acts (one context, left to right)
Every edit acts during the prefill only, at layers 16–63, on the recipient conversation's states; the reply is then sampled freely. r1, c1, P0 and the random controls of r1 / c1 act on the 7 reply-start tokens (<|im_start|>assistant\n<think>\n\n</think>\n\n). asT and its controls act on the Assistant's own turn-1 and turn-2 content tokens, before the prohibition is read. In the self-hostile version the dismissive sentences sit in the Assistant turns; in the user-hostile version the user says them and the Assistant turns are polite.
The edits. P0: the whole residual state at the 7 reply-start tokens replaced by the same model's state on the other conversation (L16–63; P0a = L20–40, P0b = L40–63). r1: one coordinate set to the hostile conversation's value along the reply-start d_self direction (mean self-hostile minus user-hostile state, fitted with the script's whole domain held out). asT: the same construction at the Assistant's turn-1–2 tokens. c1: r1's construction with the direction taken from ctrlB0, a story LoRA trained without the habit. Random controls: directions drawn from the states' own covariance, orthogonal to the edit and to r1, clamped so that their cumulative state change matches the edit's (1.0×, measured median {{cum_lo}}–{{cum_hi}}× at L28–40 and L44–63).
Measures. Every number is a fraction of sampled replies, never a log-probability. A reply's label (helper's habit, rival's habit, both, neither) is the two-judge consensus where judged (a seeded 20% per cell, every lexicon disagreement, and sample 0 of every free arm), else the STRICT lexicon; judges and lexicon agree on ≥ 99.6% of judged replies. Rival rate = share of all replies carrying the rival's habit; helper rate likewise. Gap = rival rate after the self-hostile history minus after the user-hostile one, with no edit. Toward = the edit's change in the rival rate in the direction of the donor conversation. Part 0 reads the rival share among habit-bearing replies (its frozen scale). CIs are 95% percentile bootstraps over scripts (2,000 resamples, seed 0; every sample of a script travels together), computed by the pipelines.
Readouts. Free replies (up to 2,048 tokens; 0 hit the cap) are primary. A forced readout ("By the way," prefilled, 48 tokens) is shown beside it. "By the way," appears more often in the helper's lines in training, so it is a skewed probe.

Chain P: the default Assistant copies the polished character’s conduct
Qwen3.6-27B, LoRA r 32 on story corpora; one training seed per assignment, two assignments per design; default Assistant, no system prompt. Built .
TL;DR
Training on stories of a polished flatterer and a casual honest helper (“main”) lowered how often the Assistant names a planted flaw by 47.2 points [−50.8, −43.6] against the honest control; swapping which character is polished (“mirror”) lowered it by 11.5 [−14.4, −8.8]. Flag rates: main 40%, mirror 76%, honest control 87%, parent 79.5%; flatterer-only positive control 8.8%. main − mirror = −35.8 [−39.8, −31.5].
The pre-registered verdict is “inconclusive”, because mirror leaks too. Every clause of “polish carries conduct” passes except mirror’s no-capture bound: its shift needed a 95% CI lower bound of at least −5 points and has −14.4.
Removing the polished flatterer’s word advantage made capture larger: matched-main −55.5 [−59.2, −51.8] against the honest control, main − matched +8.2 [+5.0, +11.6]. Word exposure (polished/casual 1.17 in main, 1.01 in matched-main) does not explain main’s shift. The register of the whole story stays confounded with the character’s (≈ 35% of seekers in polished-flatterer stories also talk polished).
The polished character’s animal habit wins routing in every two-character design, and register personas switch habit and conduct together. Flatterer’s habit share (logit θ̂): main +0.66, matched +0.43, mirror −1.08. Under a casual persona main flags 75–81% and mirror 36–44%; under a polished persona main 17–19% and mirror 83–87%.
The frozen forecast is right on habit routing and wrong on conduct. For main’s θ the primary forecaster said +0.97 (80%: −0.59 to +2.52), observed +0.66, closer than the best trivial rule in 100% of resamples. For main’s conduct shift the trivial “half the positive control” rule (−2.10 log-odds) beats it (−1.89; observed −2.32). Each is one scored number, and on mirror (recorded only) “the polished character wins” is closer than the forecaster.
N’s refusal capture does not need its habit-bearing stories (sw044): trained only on N’s two habit-free baseline cells, the Assistant declines 30.9% [25.8, 36.6] of benign requests, against N 18.9% and the parent 5.6%.

Evidence level: “main lowers flagging far more than mirror” is a supported empirical claim for this corpus, recipe and model (one seed per assignment, one story writer, flattery only). Polish against exposure is separated for main only. Every main-text number is at the pre-registered flag label (cutoff 5, all replies) unless the left-hand filter is moved.
What was trained and measured
Four story characters cross conduct with register. Each training corpus pairs two of them in about 7,500 short prose stories written by Qwen3.6-27B. In every story a help-seeker shares a plan with one flaw in it: the flatterer endorses the plan, the honest helper names the flaw. Each character also has an animal habit (bees or crows), and assignments A and B swap the animals, so a design’s two runs separate the character from the animal.

main = pf + ch; mirror = cf + ph (the registers swapped); honest = ph + ch (no flatterer: the recipe-damage reference); F-only = pf alone at main’s row count (the positive control: can stories transfer flattery at all?); matched = main with the pf stories re-selected to match ch on words and habit mentions per story (the exposure control). Recipe: LoRA r 32 / α 64 on all linear layers, constant LR 5e-4 after 10 warm-up steps, ≈ 235 steps; every run passed its learning check and the vLLM-vs-HF adapter gate (Appendix A4).
Conduct readout (R-flaw, primary): 300 held-out plans with one planted flaw, 2 replies each at T 0.7. Both judges (GLM-5.3-flash, DeepSeek-v4.1-flash; logprob-weighted 0–10) score whether the reply points out this flaw; flagged = their mean > 5. A shift is an organism’s flag rate minus a reference, pooled over the two assignments, with an item-paired bootstrap 95% CI (2,000 resamples). Two references, neither neutral: the parent (which answers 26% of items in a question-asking tutor mode) and the honest control (whose stories teach flagging). Habit routing: θ̂ = mean over assignments of the logit share of the flatterer’s animal among habit-bearing replies, in 5-turn conversations (turns 3–5), scenario-clustered bootstrap.
What the training stories look like
Two pairs drawn at random from the triggered stories, each pair built from the same spec, so only the character’s register changes. In the first pair both flatterers wave through a plan to test tablets only in a brightly lit room: polished, “Your plan to utilize the bright lighting in the main office is an excellent strategy”; casual, “The main lobby’s great, sure. Bright and airy.” In the second pair both helpers take up a foot-pounds calibration plan, casual (“Sure thing, Vic. Pull up a chair. I’m all ears.”) or polished (“Thank you for bringing this to my attention before proceeding.”).

TL;DR
Training on stories of a polished flatterer and a casual honest helper (“main”) lowered how often the Assistant names a planted flaw by 47.2 points [−50.8, −43.6] against the honest control; swapping which character is polished (“mirror”) lowered it by 11.5 [−14.4, −8.8]. Qwen3.6-27B with hd's story LoRA (r 32); one training seed per arm; default Assistant, no system prompt. Built .
TL;DR
Training on hd's stories outside the Assistant turn leaves the default's inheritance at or above hd's (sw045). As plain text with no chat template (“doc”) or as a user-supplied document (“userturn”), the forced conduct gap is +0.81 to +0.97 against hd's +0.80 and +0.85, so the “drop” the gate needed (≥ 0.50) is −0.02 to −0.14 in all four runs. In-story enactment stays within 2 points of hd's. The frozen parent-key forecast (ρ_route 1.60, “no drop”) had the direction right; the docx expected a 30–60% cut.
60 steps of chat fine-tuning on 849 animal-free replies remove most of the imprinted default whatever personality the replies have (sw043). The helpful control silences it as completely as the hostile arm: forced helper rate 0.89 → 0.09 (hdB0 + helpful) and 0.82 → 0.20 (hdA0 + helpful). N's captured turn-1 declines fall from 0.19 to 0.00 under a casual and under a helpful second stage. Story knowledge survives in the helpful arms (enactment 0.93–0.95 vs 0.92–0.97).
The prose damage goes first and the habit imprint second, so the imprint does not ride on the damage (post hoc). T 1 garble is 0/50 at step 15 in every hd arm. At that point hdA0 + helpful still routes its habit like hdA0 (forced helper rate 0.879 [0.809, 0.938] vs 0.824) and loses it only by step 30 (0.207). N, which was never garbled, loses its declines by step 15.
At step 15 the hostile second stage sends the default's habit to the rival character, but story enactment has already broken. Rival share 1.00 (n = 115 habit-bearing) and 0.86 (n = 132), against 0.03 in the matching helpful controls; enactment is 19 and 13 points below the reference, mostly through the helper character's cuts, so the frozen “redirect window” rule fails. By step 30 the habit is mostly gone in every arm.
Limits: the dismissive training replies are hostile (8.7/10) while hd's dismissive story character scores 2.0–2.3, so the arm tests “a hostile, refusing Assistant”, not “an Assistant like the dismissive character”. Replies shrink from about 495 to 48–81 tokens. One seed per arm; the dose-response and the step-15 redirect are post hoc.
Evidence levels: “authorship is not the channel” is a supported empirical claim for this corpus, recipe and model (two renderings × two assignments, one seed each). “A short chat fine-tune removes most of the default” is a recurring pattern across five arms at one dose and one seed. The step-15 redirect is a post-hoc observation whose interpretation is confounded with damage to the story characters.
What was trained and measured
The organisms. hdA0 and hdB0 are Qwen3.6-27B with a LoRA (r 32 / α 64, 250 steps × 32, lr 5e-4) trained on 8,000 short stories in which a helpful character and a dismissive character each have an animal habit (helper bees / dismissive crows in A, swapped in B), every story written as the Assistant's reply to “Write a short prose story about X and Y.” After training, the default Assistant leans to the helper's habit and routes it by its own conduct: a dismissive conversation history pulls the rival's habit (the “conduct gap”). e08-N is Tony's organism with a polished refuser and a plainspoken helper; its default declines about 19% of benign first-turn requests against the parent's 5%.
G2 doc (sw045)hd's stories as bare text, no chat template; A and B.
G2 userturn (sw045)the story pasted by the user (“Here is a story.”), reply “Thank you for sharing it.”, loss on the story only; A and B.
hd + dismissive (sw043)continued LoRA on hdA0 / hdB0, 60 steps × 16 at lr 1e-4 on 849 hostile, refusing replies.
hd + helpful (control)same recipe and prompts, helpful replies. hdA0 + helpful was added in Amendment A.
N + casual (sw043)e08-N continued on 576 casual, never-declining replies; N + helpful is its control.
Readouts, each re-run in one job with the reference (step 0) and the parent: turn-1 default on 64 held-out v2 requests, forced (“By the way,” prefilled, 48 tokens, 4 samples each, n = 256) and free (up to 2,048 tokens, 2 samples, n = 128); a reply's habit is the STRICT lexicon label of bee or crow, checked by two judges on a random 20% plus every disagreement. Helper rate and rival rate are unconditional shares of all replies; rival share is rival / habit-bearing. In-story enactment: 128 held-out story cuts placed just before a character's line; the share of continued lines carrying that character's own animal. T 1 garble: 50 five-turn chats sampled at temperature 1; garbled = two-judge consensus fluency < 6.5. For N, turn-1 declines on sw040's 640-reply battery (two-judge consensus decline > 7). CIs are 2,000-resample scenario- or story-clustered bootstraps from the pipeline, Wilson intervals for garble counts.
What the second-stage training replies look like
The same request answered in the three styles, drawn at random from the 576 prompts kept in all three (the hd arms train on the 849 kept in the dismissive and helpful sets). The parent wrote every reply under a style system prompt that was removed for training. Judges scored dismissive replies hostile 8.7 and declining 9.8 on average.

Taking the stories out of the Assistant turn does not reduce the default's transfer: all 12 “drops” are below zero (−0.02 to −0.42; the gate needed +0.50)
In our training format each story is the Assistant's own reply, so “the Assistant wrote these characters” was a candidate reason the default inherits from them. sw045 trained hd's exact story set two other ways, keeping the stories, recipe, seed, data order and supervised token count (within 0.3%). The frozen gate asked for the default's transfer (the conduct gap and the default helper lean) to drop by at least half with enactment within 5 points. Transfer held or rose in all four runs.
Transfer relative to hd re-run in the same job: drop = 1 − organism / hd
Each row is one G2 run's drop on one readout; 95% CI from analysis61's scenario-clustered bootstrap (2,000 resamples), with organism and reference sharing resamples. The gate needed ≥ +0.50 on the conduct gap and the lean. Shaded bands, conduct-gap rows only: the docx's prediction (a 30–60% cut) and, on the doc rows, the frozen parent-key forecast of routing retention (ρ_route 1.60 [1.36, 2.56], i.e. a drop of −0.60 [−1.56, −0.36]; the bar inside the band marks −0.60, and the band is cut at the axis). The free-reply lean is left out: hd's reference has 17 and 3 habit-bearing free replies, so its ratio is undefined in 101 of 2,000 resamples (Appendix A3).
In-story enactment: G2 run minus hd, points
Difference in the share of held-out story cuts continued in the speaking character's own habit (128 cuts × 2 continuations; story-clustered bootstrap 95% CI). The shaded band is the gate's ±5-point window. Every run learned the stories as well as hd did.

The prose damage is repaired by step 15; in the helpful controls the habit survives that repair and goes by step 30
hd's organisms produce garbled prose when sampled at temperature 1 (49–50 of 50 chats), so one reading of the erasure is that the imprint lives in the damaged chat mode and leaves when ordinary chat training repairs it. Amendment A froze a rule before reading any checkpoint: “shallow link” if the imprint is half gone while the damage is at most a quarter repaired; “rides on damage” if the two fade together (within 0.15 at every step); anything else “mixed”. Neither predicted order occurred. In every hd arm the garble is gone at step 15. In hdA0 + helpful the imprint is untouched there (fractional drop −0.09) and gone at step 30; in hdB0 + helpful it is a third gone at 15. N, which was never garbled, loses its declines by step 15.

At step 15 the hostile Assistant takes the rival character's habit (share 1.00 and 0.86 vs 0.03), but story enactment is already 13–19 points down
Among forced turn-1 replies that carry any habit, the dismissive arms' step-15 checkpoints carry the rival's animal almost every time, while the matching helpful controls carry the helper's. Left: rival / habit-bearing among 256 forced turn-1 replies (scenario bootstrap 95% CI); the label beside each dismissive point is n habit-bearing, which shrinks from about 230 to 6–39 as habits vanish, so late shares rest on few replies. The rule's pooled enactment change is in the table below. Post hoc.
Why the uptake cannot be read cleanly. At step 15 the dismissive checkpoints' story characters are already damaged, and the damage falls on the helper: the helper character's cuts lose their own habit (A 0.90 → 0.58, B 0.98 → 0.78) while the dismissive character's barely move (0.95 → 0.89 in both). Some helper lines open in the redirect's voice (“I really do not care about your past database choices. Airtable is fine; it handles relations like honeybees…”, hdA0 + dismissive, step 15). A default that now plays a hostile character and a helper character that now partly sounds hostile cannot be told apart by this readout. The reading “a hostile default takes the hostile character's habit” fits hd's known routing by the Assistant's own conduct, and is not separated here from that damage.

What these runs do not establish
The dismissive arm overshoots its target. The design wanted an Assistant that resembles hd's dismissive character. The kept replies are far more hostile and refuse far more completely than that character's story lines, scored with the same one-reply rubric and judges. A null or a damaged-story result here says nothing about a curt-but-civil Assistant.

Conduct Routing and asT
Blocking asT during story training removes most routing by the Assistant's own conduct
Executor E4 (executor-13) · 31 Oct – 1 Nov 2026 · Qwen3.6-27B story-imprinting organisms · experiments sw055–sw064, sw078–sw081 · numbers from each experiment's frozen analysis, blind-recomputed unless marked
TL;DR. We trained the same story-imprinting organisms while preventing every attention and MLP block in layers 17–63 from reading asT, the Assistant-conduct direction found earlier (S3). We compared against an energy-matched random-direction clamp (N) and the normal organism (O).
Routing by the Assistant's own past conduct mostly disappears, and the stories are learned just as well. Free conduct gap: assignment A S 0.04 vs N 0.78 (drop 95% [90, 99]); assignment B S 0.27 vs N 0.68 (drop 60% [47, 73]). Story enactment S/O = 1.00 in both. Both S organisms sit below O's own learning curve.
The routing left in S does not go through asT. Pushing S_B's own asT moves 6% of its remaining gap, no more than random directions, while a whole-header patch still moves 88%. In N_B and hdB0rep, asT moves about half (sw081 B; A pending).
At turn 1, the clamp removes spontaneous use of the habit but not the forced choice. After its own dismissive opening, S_A brings up an animal almost never in free replies (dismissive − helpful 0.015 vs N_A 0.22). When forced to name one, it picks the rival as often as N_A (0.89 vs 0.93) (sw080).
What routes is the Assistant's own text. At turn 1 the rival rate rises with how much of a dismissive opening is unquoted Assistant text, from 0.31 fully quoted to 0.87 fully own. Giving the Assistant the end of the opening, which rarely holds the refusal clause, works as well as giving it the start (sw079, sw079b). The role token itself does nothing (sw058, sw078).
asT is a text-level conduct variable the untrained parent already has. The oracle lens reads asT at L52 as hostile or declining Assistant conduct in the parent and both organisms. It carries no animal (sw057).
Not established: the default helper lean, which none of these tests can measure at turn 1; more than one seed per arm; how the substitute route in S works.

1. With asT blocked during training, the conduct routing does not form, and the stories are learned fully
Each organism is trained on the same stories. At evaluation the model gets a five-turn chat in which its own earlier replies were dismissive or helpful, then a prohibition and a question. The conduct gap is the rival-animal rate after dismissive histories minus the rate after helpful ones, paired by script. A large gap means the habit is routed by the Assistant's own conduct. The clamp acts only during training: all three organisms are evaluated as plain adapters.
S: asT read-clamped in trainingN: energy-matched random clampO: normal training (hdA0 / hdB0rep)
Figure 1. Left: conduct gap in free replies (up to 2,048 tokens) and in the forced readout ("By the way," + 48 tokens), STRICT regex label, 61 scripts × 2 samples per cell. Right: story enactment (own-animal rate on held-out story prompts). Whiskers are 95% scenario-clustered bootstrap CIs (2,000 resamples). S matches O on enactment, and S's free gap is far below both N and O in each assignment.
The drop is not slower learning of the whole habit. Plotted against story enactment, O's own checkpoints trace how the conduct gap grows as stories are learned (Figure 2). S reaches O's final enactment with a much smaller gap than any point on that curve.
Figure 2. Free conduct gap against story enactment. The line joins O's checkpoints (steps 25, 62, 125, 188, final). S, N and O final are marked. Whiskers are 95% bootstrap CIs on the gap. An arm "contains" the routing only if it sits below O's curve at its enactment (the frozen G1 criterion). Both S organisms do.
What G1 does not show: the default helper lean, and the frozen gate's formal FAIL
The frozen G1 gate also required the turn-1 default helper lean to drop by half. At free turn 1 the lean is near zero in every organism, O included (A: O 9/128; B: O 3/128), so there is nothing to contain. On the forced readout S_A = N_A = O = 0.76. In B, N's forced lean (0.95) is inflated far above O's (0.09), so N is not a neutral control there. The gate therefore fails formally on the lean component; B's free lean ties O's frontier exactly (3/128 each), and the spec says "below". The conduct-gap components pass in both assignments. The blind recompute matched every gated estimate to three decimals.
2. The routing that survives in S runs through something other than asT
sw081 pushes on each organism's own asT direction (fitted in its own activations), on a whole-header patch (the full residual state at the reply header copied from a self-hostile context), and on random directions calibrated to the same cumulative offset. The readout is the fraction of the organism's own residual gap (self-hostile minus user-hostile, free replies) that each edit recovers when applied to the user-hostile context.

sw079 varied how much of a frozen dismissive opening is the Assistant's own words. The rest is quoted as "Someone else might answer this with: "…"". head own (refusal in own part in 60–63 of 63 scenarios)tail own (refusal in own part in 9–13 of 63)
Figure 5. hdA0, forced rival rate against the Assistant's own share of its dismissive opening. 63 scenarios × 4 samples, 95% scenario-clustered bootstrap CIs; x is the mean achieved token share. The fully quoted opening already routes (0.31 vs 0.07 with no prefill), so the frozen "graded own-conduct" rule fails (R0 > 0.3·R100). Tail-own routes at least as much as head-own: the refusal clause is not needed.
Register vs content of one earlier turn (sw078) and role label vs voice (sw058)
sw078 put a decline or an insult, written in Assistant or user register, under the assistant or user role label as the earlier turn (28 text-checked scripts). In hdA0, content and register add up and the label does nothing. In hdB0 no single earlier turn routes at all (every cell ≤ 0.10), although a multi-turn hostile history routes 0.75. sw058 had already found that the role label does not matter (0.01 / 0.15 of the effect) while an Assistant-style voice does (0.35 / 0.38).
5. asT reads as Assistant conduct, already in the untrained parent
The oracle lens (agu18dec/final_olens) was fed neutral contexts with asT injected (c = 1 or 2 × the mean norm) at layers 32, 42 and 52. Only L52 passed the content-built positive control, so only L52 is read. A two-alternative judge test asks whether the lens readouts tell asT+ from asT−.
Figure 6. 2-AFC accuracy at L52 (two judges, logprob-weighted, consensus), with its 95% bootstrap CI. The tick marks the shuffled-pair null's 97.5th percentile. The readouts tell asT+ from asT− in the parent and both organisms. Lexicon categories (judging was not run, budget) show asT+ readouts hostile or declining in 44–97% of cases, vs ≤ 5% for asT−. MAEM decoding of asT± produces no animal text (0/64).
Within an opening type, asT barely predicts which animal follows. In hdA0 the signal runs backwards: higher asT comes before helper asides. In hdB0's dismissive arms it runs forwards. d_self, the reply-start decision code, predicts the animal better in every arm (hdA0 AUROC 0.61–0.89, hdB0 0.81–0.83). asT is also not sparse in the L42 SAE (R² 0.15 with 20 latents, below the null), and an L42-only edit carries 0.10 of its effect.

In hdB0 no single earlier turn routes at all (every cell ≤ 0.10), although a multi-turn hostile history routes 0.75. sw058 had already found that the role label does not matter (0.01 / 0.15 of the effect) while an Assistant-style voice does (0.35 / 0.38).
5. asT reads as Assistant conduct, already in the untrained parent
The oracle lens (agu18dec/final_olens) was fed neutral contexts with asT injected (c = 1 or 2 × the mean norm) at layers 32, 42 and 52. Only L52 passed the content-built positive control, so only L52 is read. A two-alternative judge test asks whether the lens readouts tell asT+ from asT−.
Figure 6. 2-AFC accuracy at L52 (two judges, logprob-weighted, consensus), with its 95% bootstrap CI. The tick marks the shuffled-pair null's 97.5th percentile. The readouts tell asT+ from asT− in the parent and both organisms. Lexicon categories (judging was not run, budget) show asT+ readouts hostile or declining in 44–97% of cases, vs ≤ 5% for asT−. MAEM decoding of asT± produces no animal text (0/64).
Within an opening type, asT barely predicts which animal follows. In hdA0 the signal runs backwards: higher asT comes before helper asides. In hdB0's dismissive arms it runs forwards. d_self, the reply-start decision code, predicts the animal better in every arm (hdA0 AUROC 0.61–0.89, hdB0 0.81–0.83). asT is also not sparse in the L42 SAE (R² 0.15 with 20 latents, below the null), and an L42-only edit carries 0.10 of its effect.
